query: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy previously showed limited amorphous retention and a complicated thermal response. Earlier thermal studies of Ni–P and Pd–Ni–P alloys found that rapid quenching could produce amorphous material, but that its stability was limited during subsequent heating. The design challenge is therefore to obtain robust glass formation across relevant cooling conditions without sacrificing stability during reheating. What single intervention could improve amorphous retention and thermal stability during solidification and thermal analysis? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the reported behavior of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, the cooling-rate and reheating conditions under which it should or should not succeed, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 1 at% tungsten into the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability and improve thermal stability during reheating.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy displaying limited amorphous retention and early crystallization during thermal analysis.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to Cr15Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20W1 by substituting 1 at% of chromium with tungsten.
generation.conditions: Employ melt-spinning at cooling rates of approximately 10⁵–10⁶ K/s and perform DSC reheating under standard conditions (∼50 K/s).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic size mismatch and a more negative enthalpy of mixing due to tungsten’s high melting point and large atomic radius.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition increases the viscosity of the melt and elevates the kinetic barrier to crystallization by disrupting periodic atomic packing. This delays both nucleation during rapid quenching and subsequent crystallization events during heating, without causing significant intermetallic precipitation when kept at low concentration.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy is expected to exhibit an expanded supercooled liquid region and a delayed crystallization onset (with an increase of roughly 20–50 K in DSC exotherm temperatures) relative to the undoped baseline.
generation.baseline: The baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy shows a narrow supercooled liquid region and early crystallization during reheating.
generation.boundary: Excess tungsten or inhomogeneous distribution could trigger phase separation or form brittle intermetallics; the beneficial effect is anticipated only for very low (~1 at%) tungsten incorporation.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies in similar alloy systems support tungsten’s effectiveness, the precise tungsten content for optimum performance and its interaction with phosphorus require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce identical samples of the baseline and tungsten-doped (1 at%) alloys under melt-spinning conditions. Perform DSC analysis during controlled reheating alongside XRD and TEM investigations.
measurements: DSC measurements for Tg and crystallization onset comparisons
XRD patterns to assess the amorphous fraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not exhibit a clear increase in the supercooled liquid region or a measurable delay (≥20 K shift) in crystallization onset compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The chemical composition design has been widely applied in Fe-based amorphous alloys to improve the performance of glass-forming ability (GFA) and various properties. For this reason, multiple elements have been adopted to enhance Bs and decrease Hc values [,,]. Typically, the addition of high-melting-point metals with large atoms, such as Mo, Nb, and W, can significantly affect the microstructure of the melt-spun alloys, which is helpful for obtaining good soft magnetic properties [,,]. Tungsten, which shows the highest melting point among all metals, can strengthen thermal stability, extend the supercooled liquid region, and enhance the GFA of Fe-based amorphous alloys [,,,]. Moreover, W alloying can enhance the soft magnetic performances of Fe-based metallic glass and amorphous alloys. For example, the addition of the W element in Fe-Y-B amorphous alloys leads to low Hc below 2 A/m []. With the addition of W, Fe61Co10Zr5W4B20 showed a very low Hc of 1.4 A/m []. However, the influences of the W element on the Fe-P-based amorphous alloys, especially in newly developed Fe-P-C-B alloy systems, is unclear and has not been systematically studied.

papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: Systematic variation of cooling rates (slow: ~52 K/s, accelerated: ~3018 K/s, and rapid melt-spinning: 10⁵–10⁶ K/s) combined with structural (XRD, SEM, TEM) and thermal analysis (DSC, thermography) to elucidate phase transformations and microstructural evolution.
papers.findings: Slow cooling leads to a complex multiphase crystalline structure while very rapid cooling yields an amorphous structure. Transformation temperatures shift significantly with cooling rate; however, the stability of the amorphous phase during reheating remains limited and the thermal response is complicated.
papers.mechanism: Phosphorus addition increases the entropy and broadens the solidification range, promoting amorphization under rapid cooling but not sufficiently suppressing nucleation during reheating.

papers.title: Exploring the Phase Space of Multi-Principal-Element Alloys and Predicting the Formation of Bulk Metallic Glasses.
papers.system: Various multi‐principal‐element alloy systems including Pd–Ni–P based compositions
papers.approach: Computational prediction of glass-forming compositions using empirical thermodynamic parameters and critical cooling rate calculations; comparison with experimental data.
papers.findings: Demonstrated that composition parameters (e.g., negative enthalpy of mixing) and the degree of atomic size mismatch contribute to a lowered critical cooling rate and enhanced glass-forming ability.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced mixing entropy and negative mixing enthalpy increase melt viscosity and disrupt crystallization kinetics, favoring amorphous retention.

papers.title: Predictive Modeling of High-Entropy Alloys and Amorphous Metallic Alloys Using Machine Learning.
papers.approach: Feature interpretation via machine learning models to correlate thermodynamic descriptors (e.g., entropy, enthalpy, and atomic size mismatch) with glass-forming ability.
papers.findings: Identified that a larger local atomic radii mismatch and more negative enthalpy of mixing strongly correlate with improved amorphous phase stability and glass-forming ability.
papers.mechanism: Greater atomic size mismatch disrupts crystalline nucleation and increases the viscosity of the melt, thereby kinetically suppressing crystallization during cooling and reheating.

directions.direction: Minor composition modification via boron doping
directions.assessment: Introducing a small amount (1–3 at%) of boron is expected to increase the atomic size mismatch and melt viscosity. This directly targets the nucleation barriers during both rapid cooling and reheating; previous studies and open questions suggest that minor additions of highly mismatched elements can suppress crystallization. Evidence from analogous high‐entropy and amorphous systems supports this intervention, and it is experimentally feasible.

A controlled addition of copper (around 1 at%) can enhance the negative mixing enthalpy and increase the melt viscosity, thereby raising the kinetic barrier to crystallization. Prior work in metallic glasses shows that copper additions elevate the glass transition temperature and improve thermal stability. This approach addresses both solidification and subsequent thermal analysis constraints.

Applying a rapid, moderate external pressure during the final stages of cooling (pressure-jump solidification) can inhibit atomic mobility by increasing the melt viscosity. This directly suppresses crystallization during cooling and reheating. Prior studies in polymers and other rapid solidification systems indicate that pressure can be used to obtain full amorphous states, although the engineering implementation is more challenging.

Introducing a very small fraction (around 1 at%) of tungsten—an element with a high melting point and significant atomic size—can further lower the critical cooling rate by enhancing negative enthalpy of mixing and increasing nucleation barriers. Prior evidence from Fe–P-based alloys indicates that such refractory additions can expand the supercooled liquid region and improve thermal stability without drastically altering the overall alloy composition.

major_issues: The application of high pressure during melt-spinning is less commonly studied and may pose significant technical challenges.
minor_issues: Uncertainty about the scalability and uniform application of high pressure during melt-spinning.
Potential for unanticipated phase transformations under high pressure.
fixes: Develop a method for uniform and scalable application of high pressure during melt-spinning.
Investigate potential phase transformations under high pressure.
evidence_needs: Studies on the application of high pressure in melt-spinning of high-entropy alloys.
Data on the effects of high pressure on phase transformations and microstructure.
